solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Times of qualifications

definitions.meaning: school or university periods of the year, such as the autumn one
conditions or provisos attached to an agreement

explanation.surface: A query about when someone earned their certificates.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are standard senses: academic periods and the conditions of a contract share the same word.

clue.text: Record occasion on film

parts.note: a time is an occasion, as in 'the first time'
a sheet is a thin film or layer, as of ice

explanation.surface: Capturing an event on camera.
explanation.definitionFit: A timesheet is a record of hours worked.

clue.text: Cat with no tail — or half of it?

definitions.meaning: a Manx cat with no tail at all is called by this name
it is sex, and ...-pumpy is a jokey British term for sex, of which this is the first half

explanation.surface: A question about a tailless cat and what is left of one.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a completely tailless Manx cat is also the first half of rumpy-pumpy.

clue.text: Strain to heave stone first

indicators.note: the stone letters are placed at the start

parts.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight
to heave is to retch, gagging as if to vomit

explanation.surface: A labourer struggles to lift a stone before anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: A stone is a British weight of 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: To stretch something is to strain it, pulling it taut.

clue.text: Governess's time wasted in opening pages of book

indicators.note: something wasted is lost or thrown away, so a letter is dropped from the phrase

parts.note: the opening pages of a book are its first chapter, Chapter One

explanation.surface: A governess loses time over the start of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'has' joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaperone is a woman who supervises a young charge, as a governess does.

clue.text: False rumour in article in Knave?

indicators.note: the article goes inside the knave word

parts.note: a knave is a jack, a playing card
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper story about a scoundrel turns out to be untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knave' suggests a villain, but here it is the playing card.
explanation.definitionFit: A canard is an unfounded story or hoax spread about.

clue.text: Butchery is a racket to taxman

parts.note: a bat is a racket, as in table tennis
IR is the Inland Revenue, the former British tax authority

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the tax system is a slaughter, a swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inland Revenue (IR) was the British tax collector.
explanation.definitionFit: An abattoir is a slaughterhouse, a place of butchery.

clue.text: Understanding interminable 10… 10… 10…

indicators.note: without end, so the outermost letters at both ends are lost

parts.note: the number ten written as a word three times in a row

explanation.surface: A countdown that seems to go on forever, never reaching agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: An entente is a friendly agreement or understanding between nations.

clue.text: 'King of the swingers' in love published heartfelt article

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
a newspaper ran a story when it published it
gut means instinctive or heartfelt, as in a gut reaction
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A newspaper runs a sincere piece about a famous swinger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I Wan'na Be Like You' in Disney's The Jungle Book has King Louie, an ape, sing of himself as king of the swingers.
explanation.definitionFit: King Louie in The Jungle Book is an ape of this kind, and swinging through trees is its habit.

clue.text: Team involved in row enjoyed a meal reportedly

indicators.note: as reported in speech, so a word with the same sound is wanted

parts.note: someone who enjoyed a meal ate it

explanation.surface: A rowing crew dines well after an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' looks like a quarrel but is rowing a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowing crew of eight oarsmen is named for its number.

clue.text: Notes made by yours truly on drama's cast

parts.note: a jokey way for the speaker to refer to themself, hence me

indicators.note: to cast is to throw about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone writing jottings about the cast of a play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' looks like the actors in the drama but signals the anagram of ON DRAMA, giving MORANDA.
explanation.definitionFit: Memoranda are written reminders or notes, the Latin plural of memorandum.

clue.text: Women may wear light brown golf brogue

indicators.note: the women letter is put on by, so sits within, the colour word

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Women might wear a tan golf shoe, a brogue being a stout leather shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brogue' is not the shoe here but a regional accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A twang is a distinctive nasal regional accent, as a brogue is a strong accent, usually Irish.

clue.text: Unscrupulous lawyer fakes hysteria to make case

indicators.note: the words act as a case enclosing the letters wanted, which sit inside them

explanation.surface: A crooked lawyer stages a fit of hysterics to win in court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' looks like a legal case but means the letters are encased within 'fakes hysteria'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shyster is slang, originally American, for a dishonest lawyer.

clue.text: Thing to put right later on

indicators.note: to put right is to set in order, so these letters are arranged correctly

explanation.surface: A chore that can be fixed in due course.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonight refers to this evening, a time later on in the present day.

clue.text: Unsophisticated sporty type heading into fifth place

indicators.note: the heading, or first letter, of the word is moved to become its fifth letter

parts.note: a hearty is a boisterous, sporty person, especially at a British university

explanation.surface: A rough-and-ready athlete moves up to fifth in a race.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'hearty' is British slang for a bluff outdoor sporting type.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy means robust, plain and crude, lacking refinement.

clue.text: Temperature having been taken, vet checks sick terrier dog

indicators.note: sick suggests disordered, so the letters are jumbled
the temperature is removed from the dog's name, as a vet takes it

explanation.surface: A vet takes the temperature of an ill terrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having been taken' drops T from TERRIER to leave ERRIER; 'checks' is a link, and 'sick' jumbles VET with ERRIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A retriever is a gun dog breed, such as a Labrador.

clue.text: British international and one of tournament favourites accepting court may be split

indicators.note: the favourite takes in, so encloses, the court letters

parts.note: a seed is a player ranked among the favourites in a tennis tournament

explanation.surface: A British tennis star seeded at a tournament could see the court divided.
explanation.definitionFit: Bisected means cut into two halves, a precise kind of split.

clue.text: Need place refurbished to make absolutely spotless

indicators.note: something refurbished is done over, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grubby flat requires a makeover to be pristine.
explanation.definitionFit: To deep-clean is to clean thoroughly, leaving no trace of dirt.

clue.text: Like a reckless bargain-hunter given Armani top in moleskin or the like

indicators.note: the top letter is placed within the cloth word

parts.note: fustian is a thick cotton cloth, of which moleskin is a kind

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A rash shopper gets a designer top in a cheap fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bargain-hunter' suggests shopping, but Faust bargained his soul with the devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Faustian describes a pact trading moral integrity for gain, as Faust made with Mephistopheles.

clue.text: Disapproval voiced over retrogressive atmosphere with fifty in class

parts.note: tut is the sound made aloud to express disapproval
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

indicators.note: moving backwards, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: air means atmosphere or ambience
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: A teacher tuts at a backward class of fifty pupils.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutorial is a teaching session for a small group, a kind of class.

clue.text: Fleet ferrying ambassador is hours from German river

indicators.note: the fleet carries the ambassador inside it

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy, the British fleet
HE is His Excellency, an ambassador's title

explanation.surface: A navy carries a diplomat for hours away from Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhenish means relating to the Rhine, the great German river.

clue.text: Norm? That is a spiteful person!

parts.note: the mean is the average or norm
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a man called Norm is nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Norm' poses as a man's name but is the average.
explanation.definitionFit: A meanie is an informal word for an unkind or petty person.

clue.text: Peer at gong that could have a ring to it

definitions.text: that could have a ring to it

parts.note: an earl is a peer of the British realm
gong is British slang for a medal or honour such as the OBE, an Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A nobleman eyes a medal that might sound impressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a ring to it' suggests a pleasing sound but means an earring.
explanation.definitionFit: The lobe of the ear is where earrings are pierced, so it may carry a ring.

clue.text: Wise men keeping quiet over drug taker …

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part sits over the next
the wise men hold the quiet letter within them

parts.note: the Magi are the three wise men of the Nativity
p is piano, the musical direction for quiet
E is ecstasy, the drug

explanation.surface: The three kings hush up a drug user.
explanation.definitionFit: A magpie is a bird known for taking shiny things, so a habitual thief or collector.

clue.text: Work close to home — it's not primarily for convenience

definitions.note: a public convenience is a lavatory; the singular stands for the plural block of them

parts.note: toil is hard work

indicators.note: the close, or end, of the word supplies its last letter
without its primary, or first, letter

explanation.surface: Someone works from home, insisting it is not merely for ease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'convenience' is the British euphemism for public lavatories.
explanation.definitionFit: Public conveniences is a British euphemism for public lavatories.

clue.text: … contrarily parted with odd bits of dope

indicators.note: going the contrary way, so the letters read backwards
the odd-numbered letters of each word are taken

explanation.surface: Continuing the magpie, a thief parts with drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd bits' gives P, R, E from parted and W, T from with; 'contrarily' turns PREWT round.
explanation.definitionFit: A twerp is a silly person, as is a dope.

clue.text: Writer's block previously related to exercise

indicators.note: the block comes before the writer in the answer

parts.note: an Aero is a chocolate bar, a block of chocolate
a Bic is a ballpoint pen, a writer

explanation.surface: An author once suffered writer's block over physical fitness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer's block' is split: Writer is the pen and block the chocolate bar, which comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerobic describes exercise that improves oxygen use, such as running.

clue.text: Jazzy vocalist making a meal of line

indicators.note: the singer eats, so surrounds, the line letter

parts.note: Bing Crosby was a famous crooner

explanation.surface: A jazz singer over-elaborates a lyric.
explanation.definitionFit: Bling is flashy, showy jewellery, so it is gaudy or ostentatious in style.

clue.text: Well-spoken voice put across author's last words

indicators.note: the wanted letters are laid across the gap between the two words, straddling them

explanation.surface: A clearly spoken voice reads out a writer's final message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Well-spoken' hints at a sound-alike, but the letters sit across the end of 'Well-spoken' and the start of 'voice'.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoi is a short closing stanza or postscript at the end of a poem or book.

clue.text: Look up about half of this or wing it

indicators.note: the improving word goes around the half word

parts.note: when things look up they improve

indicators.note: the second half of the word is taken

explanation.surface: Someone checks a reference, reads half of it, then makes the rest up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look up' reads as consulting a source but means get better.
explanation.definitionFit: To wing it is an idiom for acting without preparation, making it up on the spot.

clue.text: Diva rubbish? Could be — had Spooner been a Scouser!

indicators.note: swap the opening sounds as the Reverend Spooner did, said in a Liverpool accent, where the vowels of chance and pants rhyme

parts.note: Cher is a famous pop diva
pants is British slang for rubbish

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a singer is no good, in a Liverpudlian twist.
explanation.walkthrough: A Scouser is someone from Liverpool, whose short northern a makes chance rhyme with pants.
explanation.definitionFit: Perchance is an old word for perhaps, meaning it could be.

clue.text: Prompt or late restaurant reviewer consumes gargantuan starter

indicators.note: the reviewer eats, so encloses, the starter letter

parts.note: Egon Ronay was a famous food critic, now dead

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A dead restaurant critic tucks into a huge first course.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg on is to urge or encourage someone, as a prompt does.
